title: Early storm season claims hit western Sydney as brokers brace for repeat
full_text:
Storm damage across western Sydney is putting broker preparedness back in focus after the Blacktown State Emergency Service (SES) Unit received more than 50 calls for assistance over the course of Tuesday night and the early hours of Wednesday morning, November 3-4, 2026.
Severe thunderstorms brought down trees onto homes, vehicles, and powerlines across Sydney’s western suburbs, with the Blacktown SES unit confirming structural damage to several properties. The Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) has identified the current period as the opening phase of eastern Australia’s severe thunderstorm season, which runs through to at least February 2027.
“Strong winds have brought down numerous trees across roads, homes and powerlines, with several properties sustaining structural damage,” a spokesman from the Blacktown SES unit said.
Read more: BOM confirms eastern Australia’s storm period has opened
The NSW SES issued a severe thunderstorm warning covering a wide section of eastern New South Wales on Tuesday night. The warning zone ran from north of Moree, east towards Coffs Harbour, and as far south as Wollongong, according to News.com.au.
Images from SES crews showed at least one vehicle crushed beneath a large, uprooted tree. The unit confirmed volunteers would keep working through the night.
“Our volunteers will continue to work into the night to support our community,” the spokesman said.
The NSW SES recorded its second-busiest year on record in 2025, completing more than 60,000 jobs statewide. Of those, 45,000 were storm-related, and the State Operations Centre answered more than 140,000 calls across the year, according to data the NSW SES published in December 2025.
While Sydney dealt with storm fallout, northern Western Australia was recording extreme temperatures. Fitzroy Crossing in the Kimberley hit 45.1°C and the Pilbara mining town of Telfer reached 43.6°C, according to Weatherzone. It was the first time since February 2026 that any location in Western Australia reached 45°C.
Temperatures ranging from 30°C to the mid-40s are expected to continue across the state’s north until Friday.
Storm damage in NSW and extreme heat in WA within the same week present a practical challenge for brokers who manage portfolios with exposure spread across states and peril types within a single season.
The Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) reported in April 2026 that extreme weather generated $4.8 billion in insured losses in 2025, a 727% increase on the previous year. Insurers handled 294,000 claims from declared extreme weather events, and the average cost per claim rose 39% to $16,471.
The costliest single event in 2025 was a November severe storm and hail event across Queensland and NSW, which produced almost 93,000 claims and $1.78 billion in insured losses.
“While Queensland is no stranger to extreme weather, four severe events impacting a single state in 12 months is significant,” ICA chief executive Andrew Hall said.
Hall noted that storms and hail are “complex events that often have a long tail, meaning claims continue to grow months after the event.”
As of November 4, 2026, the ICA had not declared Tuesday’s Sydney storms a catastrophe or significant event. The ICA’s significant events register does not list any November 2026 weather event. That status could change if claims volumes escalate in the coming days.
Read more: Multi-state winter storm opens concurrent claims window for brokers
The National Insurance Brokers Association (NIBA) has warned that gaps in disaster preparedness remain a market-wide concern. In its 2025-26 federal budget submission, NIBA stated that “Australians are largely unprepared for these events despite recognising the significant risks they pose.”
NIBA chief executive Richard Klipin has reinforced the broker’s frontline role. “When something goes wrong, the first person you call is your broker,” Klipin said in the Insurance Outlook Report 2026.
That frontline role carries practical obligations. Martin Birch, principal at Agrisurance in Sydney, has warned that falling property sale prices can mask a growing gap between market value and rebuild cost.
“The key is to review replacement costs at renewal, rather than ‘assume’ that a CPI adjustment will keep cover adequate,” Birch told Insurance Business. He added that the renewal conversation must go beyond premium to include formal replacement cost valuations.
With this season now producing property damage, brokers should consider three steps: reviewing sums insured against current replacement costs, checking per-event deductibles on fleet and commercial property cover, and confirming clients understand what is and is not covered under their existing policies.
author: Roxanne Sanjose
